lessons.title: Body structure, skeleton, skin and feathers
lessons.html:
Body structure, skeleton, skin and feathers

Birds are built very differently from mammals. Understanding their anatomy helps you manage housing, feeding and health, and recognise problems early.

The skeleton

Birds have light bones, and some bones are hollow and connected to the air sacs of the respiratory system. The breastbone (keel) is large and carries the breast muscles - the most valuable meat in a broiler. In layers, some bones (medullary bone) act as a calcium store used to form eggshells. If feed lacks calcium, hens draw on their bones, which can cause weak bones and cage layer fatigue.

Legs and feet

Fast-growing broilers put heavy loads on young legs. Leg problems cause lameness, poor access to feed and water, and welfare concerns. Good litter, correct nutrition, lighting programmes and controlled growth help reduce leg problems. Footpad lesions are caused by wet, ammonia-rich litter.

Skin and feathers

Bird skin has no sweat glands. Feathers insulate and protect the body. Day-old chicks have down, not true feathers, and cannot keep themselves warm - which is why brooding heat is essential. As feathers develop, birds become better at keeping warm, and later more at risk from heat stress.

Comb and wattles

The comb and wattles help release heat. Their colour and condition are useful health signs: bright red in healthy laying hens, pale in sick or non-laying birds, and blue or dark in some severe diseases such as avian influenza.

Heat regulation

Because birds cannot sweat, they lose heat mainly by panting and by holding wings away from the body. Heavy broilers near market age are very sensitive to heat. Ventilation, cooling systems and water supply are critical in hot weather.

lessons.title: The digestive and respiratory systems
lessons.html:
The digestive and respiratory systems

Digestive tract

PartFunction
Beak and mouthPick up feed; no teeth
Oesophagus and cropCarry and store feed; feed softens in the crop
ProventriculusGlandular stomach; secretes acid and enzymes
GizzardMuscular stomach; grinds feed, helped by grit
Small intestineDigestion and absorption of nutrients
CaecaTwo blind pouches; fermentation of fibre
Large intestine and cloacaWater absorption; common exit for droppings, urine and eggs

Birds also have a liver and pancreas that produce bile and digestive enzymes. Urine is excreted as white uric acid with the droppings, which is why droppings have a white cap.

Why it matters

  • A full crop in chicks a few hours after placement shows they have found feed and water - a key check in brooding.
  • Gut health is damaged by coccidiosis, necrotic enteritis and poor feed; this reduces growth and FCR.
  • Feed passes through the bird quickly, so feed quality and consistency affect performance almost immediately.

Respiratory system

Birds have small, rigid lungs and a system of air sacs that extend through the body and into some bones. Air flows in one direction through the lungs, making gas exchange very efficient - but also allowing respiratory infections to spread through the air sacs quickly. Dust, ammonia and poor ventilation damage the respiratory lining and make birds vulnerable to diseases such as infectious bronchitis, Newcastle disease and Mycoplasma.

Water

Birds drink roughly twice as much water as the feed they eat, more in heat. A drop in water intake is often the first sign of illness or a water system problem, which is why water meters are read daily.

lessons.title: Reproduction, egg formation and immunity
lessons.html:
Reproduction, egg formation and immunity

The female reproductive tract

A hen normally has only one functional ovary and oviduct, on the left side. The ovary holds many yolks at different stages of development. After a yolk is released, it travels through the oviduct:

  1. Infundibulum - catches the yolk; fertilisation happens here if sperm are present.
  2. Magnum - adds the albumen (egg white).
  3. Isthmus - adds the shell membranes.
  4. Shell gland (uterus) - forms the shell over many hours, using calcium from feed and bone.
  5. Vagina and cloaca - the egg is laid.

The whole process takes roughly a day, which is why a hen lays at most about one egg a day.

Light and laying

Day length stimulates the hen's reproductive hormones through the eye and brain. Increasing light day brings pullets into lay; decreasing it can reduce production. Layer and breeder lighting programmes follow the breed's management guide.

Egg quality factors

  • Shell quality depends on calcium, phosphorus, vitamin D3, hen age, heat stress and diseases such as infectious bronchitis.
  • Internal quality depends on age of the egg, storage temperature and disease.
  • Blood and meat spots, misshapen eggs and soft shells reduce saleable eggs.

The male

Roosters have internal testes. Fertility in breeders depends on male condition, ratio of males to females, health and temperature.

The immune system

The bursa of Fabricius (near the cloaca) and the thymus are key immune organs in young birds. Gumboro disease damages the bursa, weakening immunity and reducing vaccine response. Chicks receive maternal antibodies from the yolk, which protect them early but can interfere with some vaccines - this is why vaccination timing follows the vet's programme.

Key points

  • Birds have light bones; layers store calcium in medullary bone for shells.
  • Birds cannot sweat and are very sensitive to heat.
  • The gizzard grinds feed and the crop stores it; check chick crops after placement.
  • Air sacs make respiration efficient but spread respiratory disease quickly.
  • An egg takes about a day to form; light controls laying.
